defaults.permitted_development: Across County County Durham, a dropped kerb is usually dealt with first as a highway approval issue rather than a standard householder planning application. You normally need the council's vehicle-crossing or dropped-kerb consent to cross the public footway or verge, and planning permission can still be needed for access onto a classified road, at flats, or where wider frontage works fall outside ordinary householder rights.

rules.height_rules: Across County County Durham, dropped-kerb work is controlled more by highway geometry than by a simple height limit. The council will care about levels, gradients and whether boundary features need to come down to maintain visibility.
rules.depth_rules: Across County County Durham, the real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.
rules.boundary_rules: Across County County Durham, the crossing itself stays within the public highway, so utilities, street trees, signs, lighting columns and drainage can all affect the design or lead to refusal. Boundary openings and visibility splays often matter as much as the driveway surface behind the kerb.
rules.roof_rules: Across County County Durham, there is no separate roof rule for a dropped kerb. The practical equivalent is whether the access works also introduce other structures, such as a covered entrance, taller gate piers or retaining features, which need to be assessed on their own terms.
rules.materials_rules: Across County County Durham, you do not get a householder right to choose the kerb build-up or footway construction yourself: the highway authority usually specifies the crossing detail. Behind the kerb, use a durable surface and drainage layout that can take vehicle loading without washing water onto the pavement or road.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, forming a new vehicular opening can need a closer planning and heritage review where traditional walls, railings, stone kerbs, paving or trees would be altered.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required where dropped-kerb works alter the setting or fabric of a listed building, including curtilage walls and entrance features.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.

rules.permitted_development: In Darlington, a dropped kerb is usually dealt with first as a highway approval issue rather than a standard householder planning application. You normally need the council's vehicle-crossing or dropped-kerb consent to cross the public footway or verge, and planning permission can still be needed for access onto a classified road, at flats, or where wider frontage works fall outside ordinary householder rights.

rules.height_rules: There is no normal householder height allowance for a dropped kerb. The practical checks are kerb and driveway levels, gradients, and whether boundary walls, fences or banks have to be reduced to keep safe sightlines.
rules.depth_rules: There is no set depth allowance, but the council will expect enough space behind the crossing for safe parking and manoeuvring. An access that leaves vehicles projecting onto the public footway is usually difficult to justify.
rules.boundary_rules: A dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof rule for a dropped kerb. The practical equivalent is whether the access works also introduce other structures, such as a covered entrance, taller gate piers or retaining features, which need to be assessed on their own terms.
rules.materials_rules: You do not get a householder right to choose the kerb build-up or footway construction yourself: the highway authority usually specifies the crossing detail. Behind the kerb, use a durable surface and drainage layout that can take vehicle loading without washing water onto the pavement or road.

restrictions.listed_building: If the access serves a listed building or involves curtilage walls, gates, piers or historic paving, listed building consent may be needed as well as any highway or planning approval.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.
